conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. __ from the surgery team. I hear you’ve had a lot of nausea and haven’t been able to keep much down. Can you tell me what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah. For the last two days, every time I try to drink or eat I get nauseous. I’m barely getting anything in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Have you been vomiting? If so, how many times and what did it look like?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I threw up once yesterday and twice this morning. It was greenish, like bile. No blood.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Any fevers, chills, or sick contacts? And how’s your belly pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No fevers or chills. My stomach is just mildly sore. I’ve only taken Tylenol.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How about bowel movements—any diarrhea, black stools, or blood?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: They’ve been loose since surgery, but this morning was the first formed one. No blood, not black.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Any dizziness when you stand up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, especially today. I feel lightheaded when I get up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That fits with dehydration. Your vitals look okay right now, and your fingerstick blood sugar is 88, which is fine. On exam your abdomen is soft and not tender, and your G-tube site looks clean and dry.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m worried something is wrong with the reversal. Could it be a blockage or a leak?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Given your exam and that you’re not having severe belly pain or fevers, a leak is less likely. Right now this looks most consistent with nausea leading to poor intake and dehydration. We’ll check labs and focus on IV fluids and nausea control, and we’ll keep a close eye on you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The Zofran at home didn’t help at all. I kept taking it and still threw up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Understood. We can give anti-nausea meds here and adjust the plan. We’ll start IV fluids now, and we’ll keep Zofran available. If it’s not enough, we can add another medication.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Am I allowed to eat anything? I’m scared to try.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll start gently. You were on a bariatric Stage 3 diet, but we’ll tailor it to what you can tolerate. For now, small sips of water and clear liquids as tolerated, and we’ll reassess after fluids and meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I also feel like the protein shakes make it worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s helpful. Some people do better temporarily with softer, simpler foods. If shakes are triggering nausea, we can shift toward a mechanical soft approach once you’re ready—things like broth and smooth cereals—while still trying to get protein in where you can.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’m back with your initial labs. Your white blood cell count is normal, and your kidney function and electrolytes look okay, which is reassuring. Your hemoglobin is a bit low but stable compared to prior values.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So no infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nothing in the labs suggests infection, and you don’t have a fever. We’ll keep monitoring, but right now this looks like dehydration from not being able to take in enough.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m still nauseous even sitting here. Will the fluids actually help?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They often do—dehydration itself can worsen nausea and dizziness. The other key is getting the right anti-nausea regimen so you can start drinking again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How are you feeling after the IV fluids and medication?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little less dizzy. The nausea comes in waves, but I haven’t thrown up since earlier.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. Tonight, keep it to small frequent sips—don’t force large amounts. We’ll continue fluids overnight and reassess in the morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. Any vomiting overnight? And were you able to drink anything?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No vomiting. I sipped water and some broth. I’m still afraid to try the shakes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s progress. Since you’re linking nausea to the protein shakes, we can advance you to a mechanical soft diet rather than pushing shakes right now—broth, cream of wheat, and other soft options—while we work on protein in other tolerable forms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it okay that I’m not getting much protein? I don’t want to mess up healing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Protein is important, but the first step is keeping you hydrated and stopping the vomiting. We’ll have you meet with the team for diet education so you can choose soft foods that are easier on your stomach and still help with protein goals.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Nausea is better with broth, but I’m still having loose stools sometimes. Should I worry about an infection like C. diff again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Given your history, it’s reasonable to check stool studies when symptoms suggest infection. We sent stool testing, and so far the cultures we have are negative for common bacteria, and the ova and parasite exam didn’t show parasites.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about C. diff?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The C. diff PCR test was cancelled, so we don’t have that result from this set. The good news is you’re not having fevers, your white count is normal, and your stools are improving—formed this morning—so infection is less likely. If symptoms worsen, we’d reassess.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Quick check-in: any nausea with the mechanical soft foods?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Cream of wheat went down fine. Water is okay. I’m nervous but it’s better than yesterday.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s exactly what we want—slow and steady. We’ll keep encouraging small frequent intake and keep anti-nausea meds available as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I take my regular pills? I remember being told to crush them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—resume your home medications, but crush all pills for now. That helps them pass and absorb better after your bariatric surgery changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And I can’t take ibuprofen, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Correct—no NSAIDs and no aspirin because they can cause ulcers and bleeding in your digestive tract, especially after bariatric surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How’s your pain? Are you needing the oxycodone liquid?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Pain is mild. Mostly I’m just uncomfortable. I haven’t needed much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We’ll keep pain control simple and avoid anything that irritates the stomach.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning—your labs today look stable: electrolytes and kidney function are good, and your blood counts are steady. Clinically you look much better hydrated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I do feel less dizzy. I’m still scared the nausea will come back when I’m home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a common worry. To help, we’re adding a second anti-nausea medication called prochlorperazine—Compazine. You can alternate it with Zofran as needed, rather than relying on just one.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How do I alternate them? I don’t want to take too much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Use Zofran as prescribed, and if nausea breaks through, you can take Compazine as needed. Don’t take extra doses beyond the instructions on the labels. If you’re needing them constantly or can’t keep liquids down, call us or come back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What diet am I supposed to be on now? Stage 3 or something else?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Stay on Stage 4—soft mechanical diet—until your follow-up appointment. Don’t self-advance the diet yet. Also avoid drinking through a straw and avoid chewing gum.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Why no straw or gum?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They can increase swallowed air, which can worsen bloating and discomfort and sometimes nausea. It’s a small thing, but it helps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Do I need to do anything special for my incisions or the tube site?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You can shower, but no tub baths or swimming. If you notice clear drainage, cover it with clean, dry gauze. Call if there’s increasing redness, swelling, pain, or drainage that looks or smells concerning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Am I okay to go back to normal activity?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Walk and do light activity, but no heavy lifting for 6 weeks and no abdominal exercises. You can resume moderate exercise as you feel able, as long as it doesn’t strain your abdomen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Before you go, here are the reasons to call or return: fever over 101.5, chest pain, shortness of breath, severe belly pain, vomiting that won’t stop, severe bloating, inability to eat or drink, or any concerning incision drainage. You’re stable, tolerating soft foods and liquids, walking independently, and your pain is controlled—so we’ll discharge you home today.
